VALUE on PROPERTY, PAST AND PRESENT.
Some fifty years ago an emigrant,
from Pennsylvania, an Irishman by birth,
landed at Cincinnati with the design of
seeing some of his old acquaintances who
had settled a few years in and adjacent to
the then village. He had brought with him
one hundred dollars in specie, carefully put
up in woollen stocking with a shot bag
for an outside covering. Our temperance
societies were not then in blast, and if they
had been, they would probably have failed
in proselyting him into their ranks,
for he was immoderately fond of "liquor."
He found his old associates occupying and cultivating lands, part within
the present city limits; the residue dwelling some four or five miles from town.


Both parties invited him to settle, and
pressed him to lay alongside their respective farms. The outsiders dwelt on the
folly of giving two dollars an acre, when
just as good could be bought five miles out
for half the price. The outsiders urged the
convenience of being handy to the river for
trading purposes. "If you go out to the
country, every gallon of whiskey you buy
will cost two dollars or dollar and a half."
The battle continued bravely, and each
party pulled the new settler; it was to be,
about pretty much like an undecided voter
at the polls, leaning always to the last
speaker. "Well," says he, "finally, boys,
we will take another turn, and then we make
up my mind." The turn was empirical, and
the decision made in favor of the outsiders.


Fifty acres were bought for the
sum of sixty dollars, in what is now near
the centre of Cincinnati, which after quoting the settlers laid out on the premises
have led six entire squares or blocks, 100
feet square. Five sixth of the property
was all of his holdings before came to
Cincinnati; but the one square left, without
any improvement on it, has since been as
high as one hundred and twenty-five dollars
per front foot, which would determine
the value of the naked square to be 20,000
dollars. The fifty acres he was offered
for the sum of sixty, and the twenty-five
acres in town, can still be
bought at three thousand dollars. Had the
other lot, had it been retained by the
owner, would have been now worth, at
the present value, one million of dollars.

From the ST Louis Republican, 18th.


Another party of volunteers has returned to Fort
Leavenworth from Santa Fe. They arrived on the
10th inst. and left Santa Fe on the 5th last month.
From Mr. Isaac McCarty, of the firm of Billiard,
Hook & Co. traders to New Mexico and Chihuahua,
the following interesting information is derived.


When Mr. McCarty arrived at Bosque, seventy
five miles this side of Santa Fe, he learned that
information had been received there on the 9th, that
Lieut. Brown attached to Capt. Horines company of
volunteers with several of his men, had been killed
in a small place about fifteen miles from Bosque.
On receiving this intelligence Maj. Edmonson, with
a party of his men, pursued the Mexicans, overtook
them, fought with and killed five or six of them and
captured between thirty and forty, whom he threat
ened to hang. By this energetic conduct he induced
a confession from some of them that there
was another conspiracy on foot to bring about
massacre and revolution at Taos and Bosque.


A letter was found upon one of the prisoners
purporting, though not signed, to come from the
ringleader of the former conspiracy, in which he
desired to be informed of the precise time when
Fischer's company of artillery would leave Santa
Fe as that was necessary to the maturity of his
plans. He declared in this letter his determination
never to rest while there was an American law in
New Mexico. Of the disposition of the prisoners
we have no farther information.


Mr. McCarty met the first train of Government
wagons about one hundred miles from Santa Fe.
Lieut. Love, who has charge of the Government
money, amounting to more than $500 600, was met
at upper Semirone Springs, and Col. Easton's
battalion of infantry on the Arkansas few days
previous to his meeting Col. Easton's command.
While some of his men were employed in getting
wood on the opposite side of the river, they were
completely surprised by a party of the Comanche
Indians, by whom eight of the number were killed
and three wounded.


One of the wounded was scalped alive, and was
found in this situation by those who were sent to
relieve them. He stated that he was scalped by
a white man—that he begged for his life, telling
him that he had family dependent upon him for
support but that the only reply received from his
antagonist was, that he did not care. We
regret our not being able to state the names of the
persons killed and wounded or the company of
which they belonged. It may be two or three days
before we have this information.
Lieut. Simpson, of Major Clark's Artillery battalion, was left at Council Grove, on his way home.
